author: cesare_shapable
caption: Creatine has probably collected more myths than almost any other supplement. Yes, you may gain a little weight when you start taking it. But that’s largely because creatine pulls more water into the muscle. It isn’t the same as suddenly gaining body fat. Kidney damage? For healthy people taking recommended doses, creatine has a strong safety record. If you already have kidney disease or another medical condition, speak to your doctor first. Hair loss? There still isn’t convincing evidence that creatine directly causes it. And creatine isn’t just for men trying to get bigger. Women can benefit. Older adults can benefit. It may support brain function too, and research suggests it can help cognitive performance when you’re sleep deprived. You don’t need to cycle it. You don’t need a loading phase. And you don’t need some expensive new version. Creatine monohydrate remains the most researched form. For most people, around 3 to 5 grams per day is a simple approach. A weight-based option around 0.1g per kg of body weight can also be used. Take it consistently. That matters more than making it complicated.

author: thebraintumorsurgeon
caption: @queencitylawyer needed the education. Creatine is as important for brain health as it is for muscle. We are increasingly understanding how it helps energy use in the brain, boosting cognition. What is creatine? Creatine is a natural compound made of three amino acids that acts as a source of energy (ATP)  for your body. It is critical for muscle and brain function. You get creatine in your diet, but we are increasingly understanding the role of supplementation for certain populations of people.  Studies on creatine supplementation linked here: 🧠 These studies nicely highlight major findings in creatine supplementation for women https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7998865/ https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40371844/ 🧠 This study does a large review and analysis of the effects of creatine supplements on cognitive function https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39070254/ 🧠 Creatine in a single high dose  may reverse sleep-deprivation induced decline in brain function: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-54249-9 🧠 Creatine is being studied in the treatment of dementia, but more studies are needed to show benefit in conditions like Alzheimer's, as results have been mixed.  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40395689/ https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/trc2.70101 💪🏽 Creatine has long been known to boost muscle performance and maximize benefits from exercise as these muscle stress states benefit from supplementation to speed recovery Studies look at 3-5 grams, sometimes higher in stress states and for brain benefits. It is often safest to start low under the guidance of a physician. Staying hydrated is key to safety. Supplements I take are linked in my LTK in my bio.  For most people, with healthy kidney function and good hydration, risks of supplementation are low, but always consult with your physician before starting any supplement. This is not medical advice. #brainhealth #creatine #supplements #neurosurgeon #womenshealth

author: drdavidmorris
caption: Is creatine really just for muscle? Creatine is a naturally occurring compound involved in the body's energy production system, and it's not a steroid or stimulant. Research in older adults suggests that creatine can be a useful adjunct to resistance training, with evidence for modest improvements in muscle strength. Its effects on muscle mass and physical function are less certain. Researchers are also studying creatine for brain-related outcomes such as cognition, mood, and mental fatigue, but those potential benefits are still being investigated. And what about the kidney concern? Recent reviews suggest creatine can cause a small increase in serum creatinine, which doesn't necessarily mean kidney damage. However, anyone with existing kidney disease should talk with their healthcare professional before using creatine. The bigger takeaway? Creatine may have a much broader role in health conversations than its reputation suggests. 💬 What's the biggest reason you'd consider creatine: strength, muscle maintenance, energy, or curiosity? #creatine #creatinemonohydrate #musclehealth #healthyaging #strengthtraining #womenshealth #menopausehealth #brainhealth #supplements #fitnessover50
